source_reviews.independent_solution: An ordinary optical microscope uses visible light, with wavelength of order 10^-7 m, whereas an atom has characteristic size of order 10^-10 m. Diffraction sets a minimum resolvable distance of order wavelength divided by numerical aperture (for example, approximately 0.61 lambda/NA under the Rayleigh convention). Magnifying the diffraction-limited image does not restore the missing spatial information. The obstacle is wave-optical resolving power, not merely insufficient magnification, weak brightness or an atom's motion.

coverage.evidence: q-optical-resolution alone cites source 1 and preserves the diffraction-resolution causal task, including the distinction between resolving detail and detecting some positional signal. Both intent.limitations and coverage.omitted_tasks explicitly record inability to independently write the causal explanation; no essential source distinction is silently dropped.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Every element of a wavefront can be treated as a source of secondary wavelets. At a later observation point, add their wave contributions with amplitudes and relative phases taken into account; their interference determines the resulting field and intensity. The later wavefront is related to this secondary-wave construction. Huygens-Fresnel is not just a geometrical envelope construction without interference, nor independent intensity addition that discards phase.

coverage.evidence: q-huygens-fresnel alone cites source 2 and jointly tests secondary-wave sources and amplitude/phase combination. The loss of unaided written statement is recorded in both limitations and coverage; neither part of the principle is omitted from the response judgment.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a diffraction grating with at least two regularly spaced coherent slits, principal maxima occur when the optical path difference between adjacent slits is an integer multiple m of lambda. At normal incidence d sin(theta_m)=m lambda; at fixed oblique incidence the fixed incident-angle term is included in the same path-difference condition. The slit count N does not occur in this condition. With d, lambda and incidence direction fixed, the angular positions of the permitted principal maxima therefore do not shift as N changes. Increasing N sharpens the maxima and, with the same contribution per slit, raises peak intensity proportionally to N^2. This last scaling requires that illumination assumption, and is not needed to answer the positions question.

coverage.evidence: q-grating-positions alone cites source 3, preserves all three fixed parameters and compares true multi-slit principal positions. Independent derivation of the phase condition is expressly not measured. Peak width/height were not additional source tasks and are not substituted for positions.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The selected definition explicitly interprets this task's polarized light as plane/linearly polarized light. In natural light, the transverse orientations have equal statistical mean intensities and the orthogonal electric components have no stable phase relationship; the contributing short wave trains are uncorrelated. In linearly polarized light E oscillates on one fixed transverse line and B on a perpendicular fixed transverse line; both remain transverse to propagation, and the vector arrows can reverse on their fixed lines. The fixed lines with propagation define perpendicular fixed planes. Equal transverse averages or a changing instantaneous E direction alone do not prove natural light: circular polarization rotates E but has a definite phase relationship and remains polarized.

coverage.evidence: q-polarization alone cites source 4 and definition block 2. Statistical natural-light behavior, fixed linear axes, field orthogonality and circular phase coherence are covered. Independent composition of the comparison is expressly lost. The extra limitation about producing/measuring polarization is an honest unassessed capability, not a silently omitted source demand.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Geometrical optics is an approximation when the wavelength is much smaller than the characteristic aperture, obstacle and other spatial scales governing propagation, and diffraction effects are negligible at the accuracy and observation scale of interest. Wave optics is still the underlying description. An aperture comparable to wavelength produces appreciable diffraction even for otherwise straight-line propagation; greater brightness or propagation in vacuum alone is not the validity condition.

coverage.evidence: q-ray-optics-scale alone cites source 5 and retains the relevant-scales-to-wavelength condition with the usual/result-of-interest qualification. Independent formulation of the condition and its scope is expressly lost; the statement does not promise exact ray behavior at edges, caustics or interference-scale detail.

task_fidelity.evidence: The source asks why an optical microscope cannot see an individual atom clearly. The visible stem specifies an ordinary visible-light microscope and still requires choosing the governing physical cause, among absorption, motion, diffraction and magnification. This clarification preserves atomic resolving power; it does not turn the task into retrieving a supplied numerical value.

redundancy.evidence: The four alternatives make different causal claims. The geometrical-optics question shares the topic of diffraction but asks when a ray approximation is valid, not why atomic detail is unresolved.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stem supplies neither a wavelength/atom scale comparison nor a labelled correct cause. The other questions do not assert the atomic resolution answer. Identifying diffraction over cooling or unlimited magnification still requires physical judgment.

mathematics.independent_solution: Visible lambda is of order 10^-7 m and an atom is of order 10^-10 m. The diffraction-limited distance is approximately 0.61 lambda/NA, still far above atomic dimensions for a conventional optical microscope. Cooling or enlarging the same diffraction image cannot produce resolved atomic detail. Post-key comparison: Both author source solutions identify the finite-aperture diffraction resolution limit, reject unlimited magnification and motion-only explanations, and distinguish detail resolution from carrying any position information. Their sets and every declared truth match the frozen independent findings in each locale.

option_checks.evidence: An atom is not a universal visible-light absorber: scattering and wavelength-dependent transitions exist. More importantly, the wavelength/NA resolution limit remains even when position information is present in scattered light. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The stated misconception first infers inability to scatter/emit from an unresolved outline, then attributes the missing image to absorption of all incident visible light. That mistaken inference yields the displayed absorption-only claim; the claim is false rather than merely an incomplete correct explanation.

Suppressing thermal motion does not reduce visible lambda or the diffraction point-spread width. A stationary atom's outline remains unresolved. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The stated procedure transfers photographic motion blur to atomic imaging and treats stopping motion as removing every limit. It yields the displayed cooling-to-outline prediction, which remains false under unchanged diffraction resolution.

The atomic size is thousands of times below a visible wavelength, so the diffraction-limited microscope cannot resolve atomic spatial details. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author derivation uses the correct atomic-size/visible-wavelength comparison and finite-aperture diffraction, with no misconception attached to this true alternative.

Increasing magnification scales up the unresolved diffraction image; it does not decrease the object-space resolution limit. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Equating enlargement with added spatial information yields unlimited-magnification resolution as displayed. Magnifying a diffraction blur does not add those details, so the recorded procedure genuinely produces a false alternative.

task_fidelity.evidence: All four alternatives start with secondary waves from wavefront points, then distinguish intensity addition, amplitude-and-phase superposition, nearest-point selection and a phase-free envelope. This preserves the interference component that distinguishes Huygens-Fresnel from a partial Huygens construction.

redundancy.evidence: Intensity summation and phase-free envelope construction are different wrong procedures, despite both omitting phase. Nearest-point selection is a third distinct procedure. There are no equivalent complete alternatives.

answer_leakage.evidence: Repeating the secondary-wave clause in every alternative does not label the required superposition rule. No other question states the Huygens-Fresnel construction or confirms one candidate account.

mathematics.independent_solution: Huygens-Fresnel combines secondary waves from every wavefront element by amplitude-and-phase superposition. For two equal contributions in opposite phase the field can cancel, whereas adding their individual intensities would give a positive sum. Post-key comparison: Both author source solutions retain the secondary-wave construction and coherent amplitude/phase sum before computing intensity. Their key and all per-option truths agree with the frozen independent cancellation counterexample and construction checks.

option_checks.evidence: Two equal coherent secondary waves with phase difference pi can cancel. Their separate intensities add to a nonzero number, so intensity addition independent of phase does not give the resultant. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Applying the incoherent intensity-sum rule to a common coherent wavefront deletes interference terms and yields the displayed phase-independent intensity sum. Equal opposite-phase waves falsify it.

Secondary-wave sources together with phase-sensitive amplitude superposition give the resultant disturbance and its interference pattern. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author derivation preserves both wavefront sources and phase-sensitive superposition, agreeing with the independent full principle; its misconception is null.

Contributions from multiple wavefront elements can reinforce or cancel. Geometric proximity does not remove all but the nearest wavelet. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Taking a possibly stronger nearby contribution as the only one deletes the remaining wavefront terms and yields the nearest-wavelet claim. Their interference cannot generally be deleted.

An envelope-only rule without phase cannot determine destructive versus constructive interference at the observation point; it omits the Fresnel part of the principle. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Treating a drawn envelope as the entire local-field calculation yields the displayed phase-free rule. That rule cannot determine constructive versus destructive interference, so the distractor actually follows the stated omission.

task_fidelity.evidence: The visible stem keeps grating spacing, wavelength and incidence direction fixed, changes only participating slit count, and asks about principal-maximum positions. Requiring at least two slits preserves a genuine grating and avoids the one-slit degeneration; increasing N is one valid direction of the source's requested variation.

redundancy.evidence: Unchanged directions, outward movement, inward movement and extra principal maxima are different outcomes. No other package item asks the N-dependence of grating peak directions.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stem does not provide the adjacent-slit path-difference equation or claim independence from N. Fixing the three source parameters is necessary information, not an answer cue.

mathematics.independent_solution: Let delta be the adjacent-slit phase difference. Principal maxima require delta=2 pi m, equivalently adjacent optical path difference=m lambda. At normal incidence d sin(theta_m)=m lambda; fixed oblique incidence contributes a fixed term. N>=2 changes the sum's width and strength, but not the phase-matching directions. Post-key comparison: Both author source solutions correctly make principal directions depend on adjacent-slit phase matching, not N, and preserve the multi-slit premise. They describe width/height as separate effects without requiring an unsupported quantitative intensity scaling. The frozen true set and every option truth match.

option_checks.evidence: The adjacent-slit phase condition has d, lambda and the incident direction, but no N. Holding those parameters fixed leaves principal-maximum directions unchanged. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author's unchanged-direction derivation retains fixed phase-setting parameters and changes only the number of summed contributions, matching the independent condition.

Outward motion would require a changed angular phase condition, such as increasing lambda/d. N alone does not make that change. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Falsely assuming a fixed total grating width makes added slits reduce d; then sin(theta_m)=m lambda/d would increase side-order angles. This really yields the displayed outward movement, but contradicts the explicit fixed-d premise.

Inward motion would require a change such as decreasing lambda/d. Adding slits at the same spacing leaves that ratio fixed. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Replacing center angle by peak angular width converts true narrowing into supposed inward movement. That mistaken substitution yields the option even though the principal center is unchanged.

Between adjacent principal orders the finite-N interference factor can have subsidiary maxima, but new N-dependent side peaks are not additional principal phase-matched orders. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Relabelling subsidiary peaks as principal orders yields the asserted new intermediate principal maxima. The new structures do not satisfy new adjacent-slit whole-cycle conditions and are false as principal orders.

redundancy.evidence: A concerns statistical components, C fixed oscillation lines, D sign reversal, E E/B directions, and F circular coherence. B and F conflict on whether rotating E necessarily means natural light, but that contrast is not an equivalent duplicate: one is a universal classification and the other tests its counterexample.

answer_leakage.evidence: F is an unendorsed candidate statement, not a supplied explanation or another question's accepted answer. mathematics.independent_solution: Natural light has equal transverse statistical mean intensities without a stable phase relation between orthogonal components. Linear polarization fixes the oscillation line, not the sign of E, with B perpendicular. Circular polarization gives the counterexample E_x=E0 cos(omega t), E_y=E0 sin(omega t): E rotates but its components have a fixed quarter-cycle phase difference. Post-key comparison: Both author solutions distinguish statistical incoherence from linear fixed axes and circular fixed phase, while retaining E/B perpendicularity. They agree with the independently frozen A/C/F set and all six truths. The option-level B/F contrast was already reviewed before keys as reasonable elimination, not an endorsed answer leak.

option_checks.evidence: The statement combines equal transverse averages with absent stable relative phase, matching the selected natural-light definition rather than the insufficient equal-average criterion alone. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author uses both equal transverse statistical averages and absence of stable phase relation, not equality alone; the rationale matches the selected definition and independent check.

E_x=E0 cos(omega t) and E_y=E0 sin(omega t) form circularly polarized light. Its E direction rotates while its relative phase is fixed, so rotation does not imply natural light. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Generalizing the fixed-line property of linear polarization to every definite polarization classifies rotating E as natural light. That stated overgeneralization yields the displayed universal claim and is falsified by circular quadrature components.

For propagation along z and linear E along x, B is along y; both oscillate on fixed transverse perpendicular lines. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author correctly obtains fixed perpendicular transverse oscillation lines from linear polarization and the plane-wave field relation.

E_x=E0 cos(omega t) changes sign every half-cycle while remaining linearly polarized along x. Reversal does not randomize the polarization. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Confusing a fixed line with a permanently one-sided vector treats ordinary sign reversal as randomness. It yields the displayed claim and is contradicted by a linearly polarized cosine field.

For a vacuum plane wave B=(1/c) k-hat cross E. Nonzero E and B are perpendicular, not independently selectable or parallel, including each contributing natural-light wave train. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Treating statistically variable orientation as independent electric/magnetic orientations allows a parallel pair as displayed. The vacuum plane-wave cross-product relation excludes that pair for nonzero fields.

Equal orthogonal components in fixed quadrature make a rotating electric vector with a definite circular polarization state. This remains polarized. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author correctly preserves the definite relative phase of circular polarization despite rotating direction, matching the independent counterexample to B.

mathematics.independent_solution: The usual ray regime requires lambda/L much smaller than one for the relevant aperture, obstacle and structure scales L, so diffraction is negligible at the observation scale. Large aperture alone cannot compensate for other wavelength-scale structures. option_checks.evidence: L much smaller than lambda is the opposite scale separation; subwavelength openings/structures do not generally justify geometrical-ray propagation. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Interpreting ideal zero-width rays as favoring smaller physical structures reverses the size/wavelength comparison and yields the displayed subwavelength condition, not the usual ray regime.

When L is comparable to lambda, diffraction is appreciable, so the usual negligible-diffraction ray approximation is not established. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Assuming that matching object and wave scales makes the approximation work yields the displayed comparable-size condition. Such scales do not supply the required small diffraction correction.

A large entrance aperture can coexist with a wavelength-scale obstacle or opening farther along the path. That feature still diffracts, contradicting the claim that its scale is irrelevant. A wavelength-scale obstacle behind a large aperture falsifies that claim.

All listed relevant dimensions much larger than lambda give the intended small lambda/L regime. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author derivation correctly uses separation of the relevant spatial scales from wavelength, with the stem's usual/result-of-interest qualification; the true alternative has no misconception.
